content: Cat scratch fever, also known as cat scratch disease, is an infectious condition caused by the intracellular parasite Bartonella henselae. It is generally a mild disease and is most commonly observed in children, typically 1 to 2 weeks after being scratched by a cat. The disease was first described in 1889 by Henri Parinaud. In 1931, Dr. Robert Debré identified cats as the primary vector responsible for transmitting the disease. Initially, the causative organism was thought to be Afipia felis, but this was later disproven. Immunological studies revealed that patients with cat scratch fever develop antibodies against Bartonella henselae and Bartonella clarridgeiae, which are rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacteria. The disease can be transmitted through a scratch or bite from an infected cat, as well as through exposure to cat fleas. Additionally, contact between infected cat saliva and broken skin or mucosal surfaces, such as the mouth or eyes, can lead to infection. Once Bartonella henselae invades endothelial cells, it triggers an acute inflammatory response by activating a pro-inflammatory cascade. Ticks are also significant vectors of this disease, and it is not uncommon for individuals to contract cat scratch fever alongside Lyme disease, as the symptoms—such as fatigue and headaches—can overlap, leading to misdiagnosis. Individuals who own cats are at a higher risk of contracting the disease. Immunosuppressed individuals are particularly vulnerable to the disseminated form of the disease. The diagnosis of cat scratch disease is primarily clinical. To confirm the diagnosis, serologic testing, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or indirect fluorescence assay (IFA), can be performed. High titers of immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies to Bartonella (greater than 1:256) are diagnostic. Lymph node or tissue biopsy is rarely performed. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for Bartonella in tissue or blood samples is also available. The most common symptom of cat scratch fever is tender lymphadenopathy. The lymph nodes most frequently affected include the axillary, epitrochlear, submandibular, cervical, and supraclavicular nodes. In children, visceral involvement is more common, presenting with fever and abdominal pain, which may manifest as hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Ocular symptoms can include optic neuritis and Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, which is characterized by tender regional lymphadenopathy (preauricular or cervical) associated with conjunctivitis or eyelid infection. Neuroretinitis is a rare complication. Laboratory findings can include the detection of antibodies to Bartonella through a simple blood test. It is not uncommon for individuals to have co-infections with Lyme disease, babesiosis, and Bartonella from a single tick bite. Most healthy individuals will clear the infection without treatment. Antimicrobial therapy is generally not recommended for immunocompetent patients with mild to moderate Bartonella henselae disease due to the potential side effects of antibiotics. However, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, and other antibiotics have been used, though their benefits remain unclear. Azithromycin is preferred during pregnancy to avoid the side effects associated with doxycycline. Corticosteroids may be prescribed for persistent disease. Needle aspiration of suppurative lymph nodes can also be performed if necessary.
